passage: I am Gargi, and I share a flat with Harsha. This is what I saw over two months. Harsha's rent was late, and when his uncle offered a short helping hand, Harsha said, "No thanks, I'm fine." He said it lightly, but he went quiet afterwards. A week later he told me a quick lender had given him money on the same day. The lender charged a lot, and I saw him doing sums on the back of a notebook and frowning. I can't say whether it was pride or worry; he only said, "I want to do this myself." By the third week he looked tired. One evening he picked up his phone, hesitated, and called his uncle. I heard him say, "Could I borrow until the first, and pay it back on that date?"

qa.q: Who did Harsha finally call one evening?
What might Harsha have been feeling when he refused his uncle's help, and how sure can Gargi be?
qa.a: He may have felt pride in doing things on his own, though he went quiet afterwards. Gargi says she cannot say for sure whether it was pride or worry.

qa.q: What could Harsha do to stay independent without paying heavily?
qa.a: He can accept a short, clear bridge from family with a repayment date, and keep proud independence for the long run.

qa.q: How might Harsha's uncle have felt when the help was refused and then asked for?
qa.a: The uncle offered help, so he may have been a little hurt at first but probably glad to help when Harsha called, since he was willing all along.

grounding: The protagonist refuses relatives' help to look self-made and pays a lot to a lender, then asks his uncle for a short bridge with a date.
